text: The Taliban published an 11-page biography of founder Mullah Mohammed Omar, marking the 19th anniversary of a 1996 Kandahar assembly that pledged allegiance to him. Analysts say the document aims to counter rumours of Omar's death — it details his purported daily routine — and reassert his jihadi credentials as ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi claims the caliphate. The biography covers Omar's birth in 1960 and his mujahedeen campaigns against the Soviets, but omits US backing for the mujahedeen and the Taliban's alliance with Osama bin Laden. Omar has not been seen publicly since 2001; Washington offers a $10 million reward for his capture.

Hundreds of mourners, including police on motorcycles escorting the hearse, attended the funeral of Walter Scott in Summerville, South Carolina, where the church's pastor called the killing "an act of overt racism" and family members said his death would bring change in America.

Scott, a black father of four and Coast Guard veteran, was shot five times in the back last week by white North Charleston officer Michael Slager after a traffic stop for a broken taillight; Slager was fired and charged with murder after a bystander's cell phone video emerged.

Family lawyers said Scott fled because of a bench warrant over more than $18,000 in unpaid child support, while a defense attorney suggested a reported struggle over Slager's Taser could reduce the charge to manslaughter.

Former TSA employee Daniel Boykin, 33, was sentenced to six months in jail plus five and a half years of probation with GPS monitoring for secretly filming a female co-worker in a TSA-only restroom in Nashville. Investigators found more than 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on his devices, and determined he had also entered her home multiple times. Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and a computer act violation; the TSA said he worked in an administrative role and was fired last year.

Cape Verde, lacking oil, gas or minerals, is promoting its music and wider creative sector as an engine for economic growth, with backing from the prime minister and a musician-led culture ministry. Initiatives include the Kriol Jazz Festival in Praia, now in its seventh year, and the three-year-old Atlantic Music Expo, which connects local artists with international producers and journalists. Officials hope the global exposure will boost tourism, forecast to reach 20% of GDP by 2024, though a 2013 UN report found the creative sector still small.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 at Turf Moor thanks to a first-half Aaron Ramsey goal, extending their winning run to eight games and moving within four points of leaders Chelsea, who have two games in hand. The sides meet next week in a potentially title-deciding clash. Elsewhere, Aston Villa won 1-0 at Tottenham through Christian Benteke, Leicester beat West Brom 3-2 with an injury-time goal, and Crystal Palace thrashed Sunderland 4-1 as Yannick Bolasie scored the club's first Premier League hat-trick.

Original "Twin Peaks" cast members have released a video and launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign supporting co-creator David Lynch in his pay dispute with Showtime, saying the revival without him would be "like pies without cherries." Lynch said Sunday he was quitting the nine-episode reboot because there was "not enough money offered to do the script the way I felt needed to be done." Showtime says it "continues to hold out hope" of reviving the series with both Lynch and Mark Frost; Kyle MacLachlan is the only cast member confirmed.

Andrew Getty, 47, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, was found dead at his Los Angeles home, with police saying he appears to have died of natural causes. The coroner's preliminary assessment found no foul play, and an autopsy is planned; Getty had several health issues and medication was found at the home. He had recently sought a restraining order against an ex-girlfriend, citing a 2013 diagnosis of a serious medical condition.

Maryland police say Nyia Parler, 41, arrested Sunday, cannot be extradited to Philadelphia until she completes unspecified treatment. Philadelphia police allege she left her 21-year-old quadriplegic son, who also has cerebral palsy, in Cobbs Creek Park for more than four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland. The man, found by a passerby covered in a blanket with a Bible and wheelchair nearby, was hospitalized with dehydration, malnutrition and a back wound; Parler faces aggravated assault and related charges.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Pakistani education activist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Malala Yousafzai. Mainzer discovered Asteroid 316201 in June 2010, earning naming rights, and dubbed it "316201 Malala." The dark, roughly 4-kilometre-wide body orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter every five and a half years. Mainzer said few asteroids have been named for the contributions of women, particularly women of colour.

One hundred people aboard the cruise ship Celebrity Infinity have fallen ill with vomiting, diarrhea and other gastrointestinal symptoms, the CDC said — 95 of 2,117 passengers and five of 964 crew. The cause is undetermined; two CDC staffers will meet the ship in San Diego on Monday. Celebrity Cruises has stepped up cleaning and disinfection and collected specimens for testing; it is the ship's third such outbreak after 2006 and 2013.

Trending this week: the entire "Star Wars" saga was released on digital HD, and Mindy Kaling's brother revealed he posed as a black man to get into medical school, drawing his sister's disapproval. Actors James Best, Richard Dysart and Geoffrey Lewis died, while Burger King gave engaged couple Joel Burger and Ashley King a free wedding. Also popular: Michelle Obama dancing at the Easter egg roll, Nina Dobrev's exit from "The Vampire Diaries," and Anne Hathaway's "Wrecking Ball" lip-sync.

The FBI charged Philadelphia resident Keonna Thomas, 30, with attempting to provide material support to ISIS, citing social media posts praising martyrdom and her purchase of a Turkey visa and a March 29 flight to Barcelona. She faces up to 15 years in prison. Two New York women, Noelle Velentzas, 28, and Asia Siddiqui, 31, were also arrested Thursday, accused of plotting to build a bomb for a US attack.

HBO has released a teaser for season 2 of "True Detective," premiering June 21. The new season stars Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch in a California-set story of murder, conspiracy and betrayal. Season 1, starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, was a hit whose finale crashed HBO Go in March 2014.

Carlos Colina, 32, was arraigned Monday on charges of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury and improper disposal of a body after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Surveillance video led police to an apartment building where more body parts were found; the remains were identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who knew Colina. Prosecutors say additional charges are possible; the next hearing is April 14.

Louisville basketball recruit Trey Moses asked Ellie Meredith, an Eastern High School freshman with Down syndrome, to be his prom date, arriving at her P.E. class with flowers and a Taylor Swift-themed poster. Photos of the invitation, posted on Twitter by a teacher, went viral. Moses, who will play at Ball State next year, plans to major in special education; Meredith's mother said the school's Best Buddies program has eased her daughter's struggles making friends.

NBC premieres "A.D. The Bible Continues" Sunday, a sequel to History's 2013 hit "The Bible" from Mark Burnett and Roma Downey, running 12 weeks. Also debuting Sunday: NBC's "American Odyssey" with Anna Friel, while AMC's "Mad Men" begins its final episodes. Later in the week, FX returns "Louie" for a fifth season and launches Billy Crystal's "The Comedians," and Netflix releases "Marvel's Daredevil" on Friday.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence's signing of a religious freedom law seen as enabling anti-LGBT discrimination is read as an effort to court ultraconservative voters and donors ahead of a possible 2016 presidential run.

The move drew swift backing from Jeb Bush and echoes positions from Ted Cruz, Mike Huckabee, Bobby Jindal and Scott Walker, with similar bills advancing in about 15 states.

Analysts warn the fight will pull the GOP field rightward and keep LGBT rights central to the 2016 campaign, despite polls showing growing national support for same-sex marriage.

Apple's new mobile operating system update introduces more diverse emojis, including multiple skin tones, same-sex couples and additional national flags such as Palestine.

The changes have drawn praise for reflecting America's shifting demographics, but also criticism from groups left out, including redheads and Armenians, who have launched petitions.

The author argues the update was overdue and says representations of identity, however small, should reflect the population.

Singer Avril Lavigne says she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease, telling People magazine she thought she was dying and could barely stand or breathe.

The Canadian performer, 30, believes a tick bit her last spring, and says doctors initially failed to diagnose her; she recovered at her Ontario home with help from her mother and husband Chad Kroeger.

Now "80 percent better," Lavigne is releasing a single this month in support of the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research from the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and her sister Margot died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen at least a month earlier than the previously accepted date of March 31, 1945. Researchers reviewed Red Cross and memorial archives plus survivor testimony, finding both sisters showed symptoms before February 7 and that typhus deaths typically occur about 12 days after onset. Exact dates remain unknown; Margot died first, weeks before the camp's liberation.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been charged with sexual battery by multiple perpetrators over an alleged gang rape during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. Police in Troy, Alabama, discovered video of the alleged assault while investigating an unrelated shooting and passed it to the Bay County Sheriff's Office, which says the attack occurred behind a beach club between March 10 and 12. Both men have been suspended from the university, and investigators expect more arrests.

A stray dog in Washington State survived being hit by a car, struck on the head with a hammer and buried, staggering to a nearby farm four days later. Named Theia, the one-year-old suffered a dislocated jaw, leg injuries and a caved-in sinus cavity, and still needs surgery to breathe. Her foster carer's fundraising page has passed its $10,000 target, with extra money to be given to other animals.

The FBI has confirmed Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a January raid in the southern Philippines and removed him from its Most Wanted Terrorists list. Marwan, indicted in California in 2007 and carrying a $5 million reward, was accused of supplying IEDs and training militants including Abu Sayyaf. The raid in Maguindanao killed 44 police commandos and 18 MILF fighters, shattering a three-year ceasefire and, analysts warn, jeopardising the Philippines' peace deal with the MILF.

Rep. Ed Royce argues the Iran nuclear framework surrenders U.S. leverage built by congressional sanctions, leaving Tehran's nuclear infrastructure intact while releasing billions to the world's top state sponsor of terrorism. He faults the deal's 10-year limits, citing a letter from 367 members of Congress demanding constraints lasting decades, and the absence of "anytime, anywhere" IAEA inspections. Royce compares it to Clinton's 1994 North Korea agreement, which preceded Pyongyang's first nuclear test 12 years later.

The final season of AMC's "Mad Men" premieres Sunday, ending the acclaimed 1960s advertising drama after eight years. The previous half-season concluded with the July 1969 moon landing, with creator Matthew Weiner keeping plot details secret even from his cast. CNN speculates on the fates of Don Draper, Roger Sterling, Peggy Olson and other characters as the decade draws to a close.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a roughly 6-foot-tall calf on Friday evening after an hour-long labor streamed live online by Animal Planet using 10 cameras. The newborn's gender and condition weren't immediately announced, but it was seen moving its ears, trying to stand and attempting to nurse. The calf follows a 15-month gestation and joins 4-year-old sister Jamie in the zoo's 12-giraffe herd.

Loretta Lynch's wait for a full Senate confirmation vote as US attorney general has stretched into a sixth month — longer than the previous eight nominees for the post combined. Supporters, including the NAACP and members of the Congressional Black Caucus, say race is a factor in the delay; Republicans deny it, citing a stalled human trafficking bill and Obama's immigration executive actions. Lynch's father, retired Baptist preacher Lorenzo Lynch of Durham, North Carolina, said he expected a fight, while the state's two Republican senators say they will not back her nomination.

Three people, including two police officers and a security guard, were killed and five wounded when armed assailants attacked the attorney general's office in Afghanistan's Balkh province on Thursday, the provincial governor's office said. Most staff and civilians were rescued, but gunfire between Afghan security forces and the attackers continued. Security forces were advancing cautiously to avoid civilian casualties.

Bob Barker returned to host "The Price Is Right" on the April 1 broadcast, his first appearance on the show in eight years. The 91-year-old former host, who led the program for 35 years before retiring in 2007, ran the opening "Lucky Seven" game. Current host Drew Carey took over for the remainder of the episode.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration caused by his Type II diabetes but was released Tuesday. King said he was "feeling much better," and a publicist said he was resting at home with his grandchildren. The Rock and Roll Hall of Famer, who has 30 Grammy nominations, cancelled a tour last year after suffering dehydration and exhaustion following a Chicago show.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing after two days of deliberation. Commentator argues Islam itself doesn't cause extremism, pointing instead to political grievances such as wars, occupations and repression that radicals exploit. He says the answer is not reforming Islam but showing young Muslims that violence harms rather than helps their co-religionists, a case Muslims themselves are increasingly making.

CNN highlighted its top videos of the week, including a tour of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, set to become a church, and a ride on Carowinds' record-breaking Fury 325 roller coaster in Charlotte.

Other featured clips included an exclusive interview on sexual assault allegations against Bikram yoga founder Bikram Choudhury, a shepherd's account of the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash in the French Alps, and a heated panel debate on Indiana's religious freedom law featuring Penn Jillette.

The Pentagon released a map showing coalition and Iraqi forces have retaken 25-30% of the Iraqi territory seized by ISIS, mainly in central and northern areas, though the Defense Department noted battle lines fluctuate daily.

Counterinsurgency specialist Afzal Ashraf told CNN the gains, notably in Tikrit, are significant because ISIS's claim to statehood makes territorial loss a blow to its prestige, but said Iraqi forces are relying on conventional frontal pushes rather than more effective "maneuverist" tactics they lack the technology to conduct.

Ashraf added that ISIS is offsetting losses with attacks elsewhere — including in Ramadi, at Yarmouk refugee camp and the destruction of antiquities — to sustain an image of success vital to recruitment.

A passenger on Air Canada Flight 8623 from Toronto allegedly tried to strangle sleeping Ottawa Fury soccer player Oliver Minatel, 22, with a cord about 30 minutes before landing in Atlanta on Friday. Other passengers intervened; the suspect, who claimed the team was trying to kill him, was escorted off the plane by authorities. The FBI said the man was taken for medical and mental evaluation, with no federal charges currently pending.

Hong Kong police last November found two Indonesian women dead in a Wan Chai apartment — one on the blood-stained floor, the other in a suitcase on the balcony. Former Bank of America Merrill Lynch trader Rurik Jutting, 29, a British Cambridge graduate, was charged with two counts of murder and found psychologically fit to plead. A hearing to decide whether the case proceeds to trial was adjourned Thursday until May to allow analysis of more than 200 pieces of forensic and DNA evidence.

Multiple tornadoes struck the rural Midwest on Thursday, killing one person in the Illinois hamlet of Fairdale and destroying homes and businesses. A twister cut a 22-mile path through Ogle County, where about 20 homes were destroyed — including the newly elected sheriff's — and 50 to 100 more damaged. Eight tornadoes were reported Wednesday in Oklahoma, Kansas and Missouri, with no other deaths reported; officials credited National Weather Service warnings with saving lives.

Don McLean's original manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's on Tuesday, the third-highest price for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft contains 237 handwritten lines, typed text, unused lyrics and extensive notes. McLean, who turns 70 this year, said he sold it to benefit his wife and children; the record for a popular music manuscript remains Bob Dylan's "Like a Rolling Stone," at $2 million.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit Saturday to Syria's Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp to assess the humanitarian crisis and meet Syrian officials, U.N. staff and displaced residents. The agency cites deepening concern for some 18,000 Palestinians and Syrians, including 3,500 children, trapped in the camp near Damascus. Monitors say ISIS and Al-Nusra Front control about 90% of Yarmouk, which has been largely cut off from aid since November 2013 amid reports of malnutrition and medical shortages.

Saudi-led coalition airstrikes hit Yemen's Defense Ministry Central Command in Sanaa, cutting power to 16 million people in Houthi-held areas, Yemeni officials said. About 600 people have been killed since the campaign began, including more than 50 in Aden on Monday. The ICRC has appealed for a humanitarian ceasefire, with an aid flight carrying 48 tons of medical supplies grounded in Djibouti, while a Russian draft UN resolution to halt the strikes stalled.

Former Australia cricket captain and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died aged 84, having disclosed last year he was being treated for skin cancer. He played 64 Tests, never lost a series in 28 matches as captain, and was the first cricketer to reach 2,000 runs and 200 wickets. Tributes came from Australian PM Tony Abbott, who ordered flags flown at half-mast on the day of his funeral, as well as David Cameron, Shane Warne and Imran Khan.

A total lunar eclipse is visible Saturday morning across much of North America, with the best views west of the Mississippi River. At just four minutes and 43 seconds, NASA says the totality is the shortest of the century. It's the third in a rare series of four consecutive lunar eclipses, known as a "tetrad," which concludes September 28.

A federal grand jury has indicted real estate heir Robert Durst, 71, for unlawful possession of a firearm — a .38 revolver allegedly found in his New Orleans hotel room — a charge carrying up to 10 years in prison. Durst, held without bail in Louisiana, also faces state weapons and drug charges and awaits extradition to Los Angeles on a first-degree murder charge in the 2000 shooting of friend Susan Berman, for which he could face the death penalty. He denies involvement in Berman's death and his first wife's 1982 disappearance; his lawyer cites serious health problems and says Durst is "mildly autistic."

"Furious 7" opens Friday, more than a year after star Paul Walker died in a November 2013 car crash at age 40. Producers declined to kill off his character, rewriting the script and using special effects and Walker's brothers as body doubles to complete his scenes. Co-star Vin Diesel, who named his newborn daughter after Walker, gave a tearful speech at the Hollywood premiere; Walker's brother Cody said the film is "bittersweet" but that Walker "would be proud."

"The Price Is Right" model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the winning answer during a Thursday guessing game, handing a contestant a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey laughed off the blunder as the embarrassed model tried to hide behind the display. Arbelaez later tweeted that all was fine; former host Bob Barker, 91, had returned to host the show a day earlier.

Thai Smile, a subsidiary of Thai Airways, has unveiled an Airbus A320 painted with characters from Cartoon Network's "Adventure Time," including Finn, Jake and Princess Bubblegum. The theme extends inside the aircraft to overhead bins, head rests and air sickness bags. The jet, tied to a partnership with the new Cartoon Network Amazone water park near Pattaya, makes its first flight April 4 from Bangkok to Phuket.

A mother duck and her ducklings caused a stir on a rainy L Street NW in downtown Washington on Tuesday after crossing the busy road. Pedestrians and restaurant patrons corralled the birds, with one man sacrificing his umbrella to guide the mother, while others stopped traffic. The bird family was relocated to an enclosed grassy area at 16th and L streets NW.

Investigators have gathered all main evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the French Alps and are not expected to return, French police said. A private security firm will guard the site until remaining debris is removed. Officials have isolated 150 DNA profiles from more than 2,000 samples and recovered 470 personal effects, including 40 badly damaged cell phones.

Cuba is attending the Summit of the Americas in Panama for the first time since 1962, arriving with more than 100 officials after Washington dropped its objections. Cuban government supporters and dissidents brawled in Panama's streets Wednesday, denting Havana's efforts to present itself as an open society. The State Department has recommended removing Cuba from its list of state sponsors of terrorism — a step Havana calls a precondition for fully restoring diplomatic ties — while US officials say Obama and Raul Castro may "interact" at the two-day summit.

Analysis of New Testament references suggests Jesus and his disciples lived at subsistence level, relying on begging, hospitality and donations while travelling on foot. Scholars point to the Gospel of Luke, which names women including Mary Magdalene and Joanna, wife of Herod's steward, as funding the ministry "out of their resources". Wealthy male backers such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus may also have contributed.

California regulators ordered Pacific Gas & Electric to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty over unsafe gas system operations, including the 2010 San Bruno pipeline explosion that killed eight people and destroyed 37 homes. Most of the sum is mandated spending on pipeline safety upgrades, including $850 million for infrastructure improvements. PG&E, which says it has paid over $500 million in victim claims and replaced more than 800 miles of pipe, apologised for the blast.

Lauren Hill, the Indiana teen whose battle with inoperable brain cancer drew worldwide attention, died Friday aged 19. The NCAA moved up Mount St. Joseph University's season opener so Hill could fulfil her dream of playing college basketball; she scored the first and last baskets before a sellout crowd. Diagnosed with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma in 2013, she helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research.

A large fire broke out Friday morning at General Electric's Appliance Park industrial complex in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke over the area, city emergency management official Mike Weimer said. No injuries or entrapments were reported. The cause was unknown, and the blaze had gone to at least four alarms as firefighters fought it from outside the buildings.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif received a hero's welcome in Tehran after outlining a nuclear framework deal with world powers. Zarif, US-educated with degrees from San Francisco State and the University of Denver, has publicly distanced Iran from Holocaust denial and was once among students who seized Iran's San Francisco consulate. He and US Secretary of State John Kerry face a June 30 deadline to finalise the agreement's details.

A Connecticut juvenile court judge on Wednesday denied motions to release 17-year-old "Cassandra C." from state custody and to allow visitation, her attorney said. The teen, now in remission after nearly six months of court-ordered chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, has been hospitalized since December, when a judge placed her in the custody of the Department of Children and Families after she fled treatment. Officials say the neglect petition will be withdrawn and she can return home once her final round of chemo ends, expected late April; her lawyers are weighing another appeal.

Two University of Texas researchers say computer analysis shows the 1728 play "Double Falsehood" was written by William Shakespeare and collaborator John Fletcher, not publisher Lewis Theobald. The study, published in Psychological Science, built "psychological signatures" from 33 Shakespeare plays, nine by Fletcher and 12 by Theobald, finding only tiny traces of Theobald. Scholars welcomed the objective approach but doubted it would end the long-running authorship dispute.

Marseille prosecutor Brice Robin says no videos have been used in the Germanwings crash probe, after Bild and Paris Match reported a cell phone clip showing the plane's final seconds; French investigators called the reports "completely wrong." Lufthansa said co-pilot Andreas Lubitz told its flight school in 2009 he had suffered a "previous episode of severe depression," and is sharing his training and medical records with prosecutors. Investigators believe Lubitz may have feared losing his pilot's licence over medical problems; all 150 aboard died.

American Samoan veteran Emy Afalava and other residents of the U.S. territory are suing in the D.C. Circuit, arguing the Fourteenth Amendment's birthright clause makes them U.S. citizens. The federal government deems them non-citizen nationals, denying them the right to vote. Advocates trace the policy to early 20th-century Supreme Court rulings on island territories rooted in racial prejudice, noting American Samoans are the only U.S. territory residents without citizenship.

Blue Bell has temporarily closed its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant after listeria was found in a 3-ounce ice cream cup made there, and has recalled affected institutional servings. The CDC says the strain matched a factory sample but not patients in a Kansas outbreak, where five people were infected and three died. It is the first recall in the company's 108-year history; investigations continue.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya, killing many and taking hostages, in the latest sign of worsening East African security. The Somalia-based group, which pledged allegiance to al Qaeda in 2012, has staged cross-border raids in Kenya since 2011, including the 2013 Westgate mall massacre. Analysts say military action alone won't stop it, as poverty, corruption, poor governance and exclusion continue to fuel recruitment.

The U.S. is filing a diplomatic complaint with Moscow after a Russian SU-27 intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea on Tuesday, in what the Pentagon called an "unsafe and unprofessional" manner. Russia's Defense Ministry said the U.S. plane was heading toward its border with its transponder off, a claim U.S. European Command denied. A similar incident occurred a year ago over the Sea of Okhotsk, when a Russian jet flew within 100 feet of a U.S. plane.

North Charleston artist Phillip Hyman created a black-winged hooded angel from reclaimed wood and house paint after Walter Scott, an unarmed black man, was fatally shot in the back by a white police officer on Saturday. He placed the piece near the shooting site on Tuesday. Black Lives Matter protesters asked to use it and carried it at a rally outside City Hall, where it was widely photographed.

Eyewitness video of North Charleston, South Carolina, officer Michael Slager fatally shooting unarmed black man Walter Scott has exposed discrepancies in initial police accounts. Slager, who said Scott seized his Taser, has been fired and charged with murder; witness Feidin Santana says Scott never took the weapon. Police reports also conflict over whether CPR was performed on Scott, and the department has declined further comment citing a state investigation.

ISIS said it stormed Iraq's largest oil refinery at Baiji late Saturday and by Sunday claimed to control several buildings inside the facility. Iraqi security officials denied the claim, saying government forces retain full control; CNN could not verify the militants' assertions. The refinery, which supplies much of Iraq's domestic fuel, lies 40 kilometres from Tikrit, retaken from ISIS less than two weeks ago.

Nashville's district attorney has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, after the option was used four times in five years, sparking public outrage. Commentators note sterilization plea bargains, largely involving male defendants, have long been used across the US and are likely constitutional, since defendants can waive constitutional rights. Analysts suggest gender bias explains why the female case drew outrage while male castration deals went largely unnoticed.

More than 25,000 people have been infected with Ebola over the past year, with over 10,000 deaths, in what the WHO called the most severe public health emergency of modern times. New cases have fallen sharply, with 30 confirmed in the week of April 5 — the lowest weekly total since May 2014 — and surplus treatment facilities in Liberia and Sierra Leone now being decommissioned. But Guinea reported unsafe burials and deaths identified as Ebola only post-mortem, suggesting undetected transmission chains could fuel new infections.

The NCAA says in a court filing it has no legal duty "to ensure the academic integrity of the courses offered to student-athletes," responding to a lawsuit by former University of North Carolina athletes caught in an 18-year academic fraud scheme involving fake classes. Critics, including whistleblower Mary Willingham and attorney Michael Hausfeld, say the stance contradicts the NCAA's longstanding claim that athletes are "students first" and are compensated with an education. The NCAA likened its role to that of the American Bar Association, while UNC, also sued, has admitted the fraud but asked that the case be dismissed as untimely.

An explosion at a paraxylene chemical plant in Zhangzhou, Fujian province, injured six people Monday night, sparking a large fire, Chinese state media reported. The blast occurred at an oil storage facility after a leak; five people were hurt by broken glass, and no toxic spill has been reported. Over 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control by Tuesday morning at the plant, which was relocated from Xiamen after 2007 protests and suffered a previous explosion in 2013.

Op-ed argues the bystander video of Officer Michael Slager shooting Walter Scott in the back in North Charleston is the only reason the case will see justice. The writer, a defense attorney, says a police body camera would likely have prevented the killing, and that studies show cameras reduce complaints and use-of-force incidents. He calls cameras an interim fix for deeper racial bias in policing, urging tougher hiring screens, more training and broader social reform.

Leaders from 35 Western Hemisphere nations gather in Panama City for the VII Summit of the Americas, where Obama and Cuba's Raul Castro are expected to meet for the first time since December's détente. Venezuela has overshadowed the thaw, with President Nicolas Maduro accusing Washington of plotting his overthrow and campaigning to repeal US sanctions on seven Venezuelan officials. Cuba's foreign minister has publicly backed Maduro, and it remains unclear how many other Latin American leaders will follow.

A nuclear submarine under repair at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard in the country's northwest caught fire, Russian news agencies reported. Rubber insulation between the hulls ignited during welding work while the vessel was in dry dock. Officials said nuclear fuel had been removed and no weapons or hazardous materials were aboard; personnel were evacuated and no injuries were reported.

Tropical storm Maysak — known locally as Chedeng — is bearing down on the Philippines, prompting flash flood and landslide warnings. The system, a super typhoon days ago with 150 mph winds, has weakened to sustained winds above 70 mph with gusts to 90 mph. Officials have banned water activities in some areas and ordered precautionary evacuations, with landfall expected Sunday morning in Isabela province.

NFL Hall of Famer Deion Sanders publicly mocked his son on Twitter after the younger Sanders said he only eats "hood doughnuts." Sanders reminded his 912,000 followers that Deion Sanders Jr. has a million-dollar trust fund, a condo and his own clothing line, tweeting: "You're a Huxtable with a million $ trust fund. Stop the hood stuff!" Sanders Jr., a wide receiver at Southern Methodist University, retweeted his father's jabs.

Guatemala ranks third worldwide in killings of women, with two women murdered daily and 98% of homicide cases never reaching court, according to UN figures. Activists blame the legacy of the country's 36-year civil war, entrenched machismo, corrupt police and weak courts, and the spread of drug cartels and gangs.

Abuse survivor Adelma Cifuentes, who lost an arm in an attack ordered by her husband, secured his 27-year sentence and now performs in a play with other survivors. The government has passed a femicide law and created specialized courts, while NGOs and girls' programs work to change social norms.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring residents to submit "mugshots" of their cattle along with details of distinguishing features such as coloring, age and tail length, to build a database for enforcing Maharashtra's new beef ban. Over 100 owners have complied since the law made killing cows, bulls and bullocks a non-bailable offense punishable by up to five years in prison. Beef traders, who ended a month-long strike Wednesday, plan to challenge the ban in the state high court.

Police in Lucknow, northern India, have purchased four pepper-spray drones to control violent protests and mob attacks, with a fifth on order. Each drone, fitted with a camera and pepper spray, costs between $9,560 and $19,300. Critics warn the measure could suppress free speech and reflects a preference for force over dialogue, with an official launch expected later this month.

Christie's sold the 16-page handwritten manuscript of Don McLean's "American Pie" lyrics for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer on Tuesday. McLean wrote the 8½-minute song, released in November 1971, partly in response to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. The Recording Industry Association of America and the National Endowment for the Arts ranked it the fifth greatest song of the 20th century.

Thieves broke into a safety deposit vault in London's Hatton Garden jewellery district over the Easter weekend, in a raid compared to the 1971 Baker Street bank tunnel burglary.

Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm says such heists require months of planning, cloned vehicles, forensic clean-ups and usually inside information, and are motivated solely by money.

Detectives are examining possible insider involvement, CCTV, vehicle movements and forensic traces, while informers are tasked and stolen item details circulated to markets at home and abroad.

7-Eleven held its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday at participating US stores from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., letting customers fill any container for $1.49. In-store displays with a 10-inch-diameter hole limited cup size, and containers had to be sanitary. The promotion is separate from the chain's annual Free Slurpee Day on July 11.

Georgia Powers, the first woman and first person of color elected to the Kentucky State Senate, dismisses Rand Paul's presidential launch and his claim to be broadening the GOP's appeal to minority voters. She cites his questioning of the Civil Rights Act, his opposition to a stronger Voting Rights Act, his call to abolish the Education Department, and his stances on abortion and DREAMers. Powers says his record is "outdated" and disqualifying, and that "the American people deserve better."

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail Sunday at the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway, killing passenger Gary Terry, 36, of Davenport, Florida. Driver Tavon Watson, 24, of Kissimmee lost control of the car and was hospitalized with minor injuries, Florida Highway Patrol said. Operator Petty Holdings extended sympathies to those involved in the "tragic accident."

The defense in Aaron Hernandez's murder trial rested after less than a day, following months of prosecution testimony from 131 witnesses. Closing arguments in the case over the 2013 shooting death of Odin Lloyd are set for Tuesday, with much of the evidence circumstantial, including disputed footwear impressions and grainy security video prosecutors say shows a handgun. The former Patriots tight end has pleaded not guilty and faces a separate double-murder trial in Boston.

Chinese authorities have formally detained women's rights activist Wu Rongrong and four others for "creating disturbances" after they planned an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment. By April 13 the five must be released or formally arrested, which in China almost always results in conviction. The detentions come as Beijing prepares an anti-domestic violence law and marks the 20th anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women, amid a broader crackdown on independent activism.

Former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley told reporters in Iowa that Hillary Clinton's status as Democratic frontrunner is not unassailable, saying "history is full of examples where the inevitable frontrunner was inevitable right up until" they weren't. O'Malley, who called Clinton an "eminently qualified candidate" but avoided direct attacks, polls at about 1% nationally and in Iowa, while Clinton leads by more than 40 points. Clinton is expected to launch her campaign Sunday via a social media video.

Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison Wednesday in Fall River, Massachusetts, for the June 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd, 27.

Lloyd's mother, sister and uncle gave victim impact statements, describing him as a devoted family man, athlete and hard worker.

His mother, Ursula Ward, said she forgave those involved in her son's murder and urged others to do the same.

Ted Cruz made his first Iowa swing as a declared presidential candidate, courting the state's large evangelical bloc with talk of his faith, his pastor father and defence of Indiana's "religious freedom" law. His first TV ads, airing around Easter, cite the "transformative love of Jesus Christ". Advisers say evangelicals are one of three target groups alongside tea party and libertarian voters, though rivals including Huckabee, Santorum, Bush, Walker, Carson, Rubio and Paul are also vying for religious conservatives.

Marvel released a poster revealing Paul Bettany as the android Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and unveiled video of Charlie Cox's red suit ahead of the Netflix series "Daredevil."

Director Bryan Singer told Empire that Ben Hardy will play the winged mutant Angel in next year's "X-Men: Apocalypse," sharing a photo of the character.

A first look at Jamie Bell's CGI version of The Thing in the "Fantastic Four" reboot, due August 7, also emerged, along with a new image of Ryan Reynolds in "Deadpool."

Italy's Coast Guard says 978 migrants were rescued Friday in the Mediterranean, about 30 miles off Libya's coast. More than 10,000 migrants reached Italy in the first quarter of 2015, the IOM said, with roughly 2,000 rescued in the Channel of Sicily in early April. At least 480 have died crossing the Mediterranean this year, up from fewer than 50 at the same point in 2014.

French-language global broadcaster TV5Monde regained control of one of its 11 channels Thursday after what its director called an "extremely powerful cyberattack" knocked out its broadcasts, websites and social media accounts. ISIS logos appeared on the network's social media accounts, and the network said on a mobile site it had been "hacked by an Islamist group," though no group claimed responsibility. TV5Monde reaches 260 million homes worldwide and operates through a partnership involving the governments of France, Canada and Switzerland.

David Lynch says he will not direct the revival of "Twin Peaks," citing insufficient funding from the network. The director announced his exit on Twitter, adding he had personally phoned cast members over the weekend. Showtime, which has ordered nine episodes, said it was "saddened" and hopes Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost will still be involved.

Jurors in Boston began deliberating Tuesday on 30 charges against Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who faces life in prison or execution if convicted in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing. Closing arguments were set in Fall River, Massachusetts, in the murder trial of ex-Patriot Aaron Hernandez, accused of killing Odin Lloyd. Senator Rand Paul launched his presidential bid in Louisville, while voters in Chicago cast ballots in a mayoral runoff between Rahm Emanuel and Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, and Ferguson, Missouri, held council elections in the wake of Michael Brown's death.

Tornado sirens sounded across Kansas on Wednesday night as spotters reported twisters near Goddard, west of Wichita, and in the state's southwest near Aetna. The National Weather Service said a tornado may also have touched down in Potosi, Missouri, where wind damage, flooding and baseball-sized hail were reported. Further storms were forecast Thursday for the Midwest, Mississippi and Tennessee river valleys and southern Great Lakes.

Jodi Arias was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of release for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. The judge decided the sentence after two juries deadlocked on whether to impose the death penalty, taking execution off the table. Arias, 34, told the court she was "disgusted and repulsed" with herself; she will serve her term at a state prison near Goodyear, Arizona.

The EPA said preliminary tests found methyl bromide, a highly toxic pesticide banned for indoor use, in a St. John villa where a Delaware family of four fell ill and were hospitalised after a March stay. Investigators are examining whether a March 18 fumigation at the Sirenusa resort caused the illnesses and whether laws were broken. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Terminix, which provided the pest control services.

A Columbia Journalism School review found "institutional failure" at Rolling Stone over its discredited University of Virginia gang-rape story, prompting an apology from managing editor Will Dana. Phi Kappa Psi has said it will pursue legal action. Legal analysts note UVA cannot sue as a public entity, while the fraternity would have to prove the story defamed identifiable individuals and caused measurable harm.

FBI agents shot and wounded Kevone Charleston, 36, of Austell, Georgia, as he allegedly attempted to rob a CVS in Forsyth County early Saturday. Two agents were injured when the suspect rammed government vehicles during his attempted escape, overturning an SUV; both were treated and released. Charleston, suspected in 32 commercial robberies since November 2013, is in custody with non-life-threatening injuries.

Alaska Airlines Flight 448 from Seattle to Los Angeles made an emergency landing Monday after the pilot and passengers heard banging and faint screams from the cargo hold. A ramp agent employed by contractor Menzies Aviation had fallen asleep inside the pressurized hold; he was hospitalized as a precaution, passed a drug test and was released. The flight, carrying 170 passengers and six crew, later reached Los Angeles; the airline is investigating.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks, charged with killing three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill in February, is eligible for the death penalty. Hicks, 46, the victims' neighbor, was indicted on three counts of first-degree murder over the shooting deaths of Yusor Mohammad, her husband Deah Shaddy Barakat and her sister Razan Mohammad Abu-Salha. Police cited a parking dispute as a possible factor, while the victims' families and federal investigators are examining whether it was a hate crime.

Amnesty International's report "Their Lives on the Line" says women's rights activists in Afghanistan face attacks from the Taliban, warlords and government officials, with perpetrators rarely punished. The group says Afghan authorities offer female defenders less protection than male colleagues, and police stood by during the mob killing of Farkhunda in Kabul. Activists say the funeral, at which women carried the coffin for the first time, has galvanised the women's movement.

A New York judge has permitted a woman to serve divorce papers on her elusive husband via Facebook private message. Commentators note traditional alternatives, such as nailing documents to a door or publishing legal notices in obscure journals, are often less reliable than electronic contact. Service by private message or email remains private, though online service is expected to expand further.

The Rev. Robert H. Schuller, the California televangelist who founded the "Hour of Power" broadcast and the Crystal Cathedral megachurch, died Thursday at 88, his family said. He had been diagnosed with esophageal cancer in August 2013. Schuller built a following with an upbeat "possibility thinking" gospel, but his ministry collapsed amid a family succession dispute and a 2010 bankruptcy filing citing more than $43 million in debts.

Four workers were killed and 45 injured, two seriously, in a fire on Pemex's Abkatun Permanente oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico's Campeche Sound on Wednesday. About 300 people were evacuated and at least 10 boats fought the blaze, which was extinguished by Wednesday night. Pemex denied reports the platform collapsed, said there was no oil spill, and has not given a cause.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed a law Tuesday banning "dismemberment abortion," the first such measure in the United States. The law prohibits the dilation and evacuation procedure commonly used in the second trimester, with an exception to protect the mother's life or health. National Right to Life called it a model for other states, while Planned Parenthood said Kansas now has more abortion restrictions than any other state.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said it will investigate popular host Bi Fujian after a leaked video showed him cursing Mao Zedong at a private dinner party, calling the late leader an "old son of a b***h." Bi apologized on Weibo, saying his remarks had "grave social consequences." The clip has been scrubbed from Chinese video sites and split opinion online, with some demanding punishment and others saying he was set up.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using an expletive and a racial slur about Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky following Kentucky's Final Four loss Saturday. Harrison, who is black, said the remark about Kaminsky, who is white, was made "in jest" and phoned him to apologize. Kaminsky said Sunday he was "over it" ahead of Monday's title game against Duke.

"Arrested Development" executive producer Brian Grazer says the comedy will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes, revealing the news on Bill Simmons' podcast. Netflix declined to comment to CNN. The show's fourth season streamed on Netflix in 2013 after Fox canceled it; it is unclear whether the full cast will return.

The Large Hadron Collider has resumed operations after a two-year shutdown, with the first beams circulating Sunday through its 17-mile ring at CERN near Geneva. Scientists aim to recreate conditions just after the Big Bang to probe the origin of mass, dark matter and antimatter. The next step is raising beam energy to record levels, officials said.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of an armed U.S. Navy MH-60R helicopter over the Persian Gulf this month, U.S. officials told CNN. No shots were fired and the helicopter deliberately broke away, but officials worry the unsafe maneuver was ordered locally, raising fears Iran's commanders lack full control of forces in the region. Washington is weighing a formal protest; the incident coincided with nuclear talks in Switzerland and U.S. patrols watching for Iranian arms shipments to Yemen's Houthi rebels.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty Wednesday on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial after jurors deliberated for 11½ hours. Seventeen of the counts carry the possibility of the death penalty, and the case now moves to a penalty phase with a start date yet to be set. His lawyers, who conceded he was present, argued his older brother Tamerlan was the plot's instigator.

Indian police arrested four employees of ethnic-wear chain FabIndia after federal education minister Smriti Irani spotted a surveillance camera pointed at a changing room in a Goa store. Investigators confirmed the camera could photograph customers in the changing room; the store was sealed and the manager remained at large. The staff face voyeurism and privacy breach charges carrying up to three years in jail. FabIndia said it was "shocked" and would cooperate with police.

Iran will lift its ban on women attending some men's sports events within the next year, Deputy Sports Minister Abdolhamid Ahmadi said, with restrictions reportedly eased for indoor events. Women have been barred from most men's sports since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, with a brief exception for volleyball under President Khatami. The move follows international pressure, including FIFA President Sepp Blatter's criticism of the "intolerable" ban and Iran's failed bid to host the 2019 Asian Cup.

Indian software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in jail over India's biggest corporate fraud in memory, police said. Raju, former chairman of Satyam Computer Services, was also fined $804,000 after admitting in 2009 to inflating profits with fictitious assets in a $1.6 billion scam. Satyam was then India's fourth-largest software services provider; it was later sold to Tech Mahindra after the government fired its board.

Alaska Airlines has apologised after removing cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a Hawaii flight because she lacked a doctor's note clearing her to fly. Sedway said she was treated "as if I'm a criminal or contagious" after telling a crew member she sometimes felt weak. The airline said staff consulted its medical advisory service with her wellbeing in mind, but conceded the matter "could have been handled differently"; it refunded her family's tickets and paid for their overnight accommodation. Sedway, who flew home to San Jose late Tuesday, said the delay caused her to miss a chemotherapy session.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan Acar died of cancer Friday in an Istanbul hospital at age 66, five days after his birthday. First diagnosed in 1990, the year he placed 17th at the Eurovision Song Contest, he saw the disease return in 2005 and 2014. Known for his love songs, he recorded nearly 20 albums, with 1991's "I Made a Vow" his most popular; his last performance was in Istanbul on Valentine's Day.

Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu criticised the framework nuclear deal between Iran and six world powers on CNN's "State of the Union," saying a third option exists beyond "this bad deal or war" — maintaining pressure to secure better terms. He said the deal leaves Iran's nuclear infrastructure intact and that Tehran, guilty of "congenital cheating," cannot be trusted.

Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein said she wished Netanyahu "would contain himself," calling the deal "on the cusp of something that can be workable," while Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz said it extends Iran's breakout time from two months to a year. Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham urged keeping sanctions for two years until a new president takes office.

A security guard was shot and critically wounded outside the U.S. Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, Maryland, on Thursday after approaching a vehicle in which two people were arguing. The suspect fled, firing at multiple locations during a police chase that ended in a crash and shootout on Washington's H Street, wounding an officer and the suspect. Police said the incident began as a domestic kidnapping; the victim was found in good condition.

Chelsea Manning, serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, has joined Twitter, quickly gaining more than 26,000 followers. Barred from internet access, she dictates tweets by phone to Fitzgibbon Media, which posts them on her behalf. Manning, who announced her gender transition in 2013, is receiving authorized hormone therapy at Fort Leavenworth and has previously written op-eds from prison.

Rapper Nelly was arrested on drug charges in Putnam County, Tennessee, after a state trooper stopped his tour bus on Interstate 40 for missing regulatory stickers and smelled marijuana. Troopers searched the bus and found methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia, several handguns and 100 small Ziploc bags. Nelly, 40, whose real name is Cornell Haynes, was charged with felony drug possession and released on bond.

A Delaware father is in stable condition while his two teenage sons remain critical after the family fell ill at a rented villa at the Sirenusa resort in St. John, U.S. Virgin Islands. EPA preliminary tests found methyl bromide, a highly toxic pesticide banned for indoor use, in the unit; the boys' mother was treated and released. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation, and the rental agent has cut ties with pest-control firm Terminix.

Bloggers and online journalists across Asia face rising legal and physical threats as governments curb Internet freedom through defamation suits, restrictive laws and imprisonment. Recent cases include teenage blogger Amos Yee's arrest in Singapore, the detention of five Malaysian Insider staff in Malaysia, and mass jailings in China and Vietnam. In Bangladesh, Washiqur Rahman Babu became the second blogger hacked to death in five weeks, following the killing of Avijit Roy, with such murders rarely resulting in convictions.

Actress Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving The CW's "Vampire Diaries" at the end of the current season, after six years playing Elena Gilbert. Fans reacted angrily, questioning the show's renewal for a seventh season and the fate of the "Delena" romance. Producer Julie Plec backed Dobrev's decision, saying the series will continue focusing on the Salvatore brothers.

Conditions in Damascus' Yarmouk camp have worsened since ISIS fighters stormed the Palestinian district two weeks ago, prompting government shelling and barrel bombing, residents say. ISIS has since withdrawn, leaving al Qaeda-linked Jabhat al-Nusra in control, an activist told CNN. About 18,000 of the camp's original 100,000-plus residents remain, largely cut off from food, water and aid, according to UNRWA.

NASA scientists last week outlined plans to search for life beyond Earth over the coming decades, following the discovery of nearly 2,000 exoplanets since 1995. Astronomers estimate the Milky Way may hold some 40 billion Earth-like, habitable-zone planets, though only a tiny fraction would ever host radio-capable civilizations — and likely not at the same time as humans. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, launching in 2018, will hunt for biological signatures in exoplanet atmospheres, while missions to Mars and Jupiter's moons Europa and Ganymede will probe for simpler life forms.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina, 32, will be arraigned April 14 on a murder charge after human remains were found Saturday in a duffel bag in Cambridge, prosecutors said. Police found additional body parts in a nearby apartment building after reviewing surveillance video; the remains were identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who knew Colina. Colina was earlier arraigned on assault and battery and improper disposal of a body charges, and a judge revoked his bail in a separate assault case.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit brought by paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he attacked at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2013. Attorney Gloria Allred said the settlement included an apology from West, and released a photo of the two shaking hands. West previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanour battery over the incident and was sentenced to two years' probation, anger management and community service.

Opinion piece argues Obama's political stake in an Iran nuclear deal — central to his foreign policy legacy since his 2007 campaign pledge to meet Iranian leaders "without preconditions" — has left Washington appearing the more desperate party and weakened its negotiating position. The framework announced Thursday falls far short of Obama's 2012 vow that Iran would "end their nuclear program," allowing Tehran to keep about a third of its 6,000-plus centrifuges, retain facilities including a converted Fordow, and see sanctions eased almost immediately. Critics cite Iran's record of concealment from U.N. inspectors, Saudi threats to pursue nuclear weapons, and the war in Yemen as evidence the accord leaves Iran a nuclear threshold state with a one-year breakout period.

Bystander video contradicted North Charleston officer Michael Slager's account of fatally shooting Walter Scott, leading to his arrest on murder charges. The case highlights the lack of national data on police killings, despite a 1994 law requiring the Justice Department to collect and publish it. Media investigations and activist databases have filled some gaps, and Obama's policing task force has again urged comprehensive federal data collection.

Five American aid workers monitored for Ebola exposure in Sierra Leone have been released from an Omaha, Nebraska, hospital after three weeks, Nebraska Medicine said. None developed the virus; one was discharged after an unrelated heart issue and remains in the area. The clinicians, from Boston-based Partners in Health, had contact with an infected colleague now in fair condition at the NIH in Maryland.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars spent a 13th week atop the Billboard Hot 100, the longest run of the 2010s, surpassing Robin Thicke's "Blurred Lines." It becomes one of only 10 singles to lead the chart for at least 13 weeks since 1958, trailing the record 16 weeks held by Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men's "One Sweet Day." Newcomer Natalie La Rose entered the top 10 at No. 10 with her debut "Somebody," featuring Jeremih.

Twitter fans marked "Rex Manning Day" on April 8, a nod to the 1995 film "Empire Records," coinciding with a "Lost" anniversary date.

CNN lists other dates immortalised by movies, including April 14 from "Titanic," April 25 from "Miss Congeniality," and October 3, known as "Mean Girls Day."

October 21, 2015, is also flagged as the date Marty McFly travels to in "Back to the Future Part II."

Nicole Kidman's "Grace of Monaco" will skip U.S. theaters and premiere on Lifetime on May 25. The Weinstein Co., which bought U.S. rights, opted to sell to the cable network after the critically panned film flopped internationally following its Cannes opening. The production was dogged by a public feud between director Olivier Dahan and Harvey Weinstein over the final cut, and by criticism from Grace Kelly's children, who called it historically inaccurate.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance Wednesday allowing "partnership certificates" for same-sex couples, granting hospital visitation and joint tenancy rights. The certificates, to be issued later in the summer, are not legally binding, and benefits like joint tax filing remain under federal control. Activists called it a first step but said national legislation is needed for equal rights; neighbouring Setagaya ward may follow suit.

California's four-year drought is a national concern, as the state produces more than a third of US vegetables and nearly two-thirds of its fruits and nuts; prices for berries, grapes, broccoli and other produce rose last year. Fresh fruit prices are projected to rise 2.5-3.5% this year, though a strong dollar and cheap oil may offset drought effects, while Western drought conditions drove beef and veal prices up 12.1% in 2014. Tourists face water served only on request, laundry restrictions and early ski resort closures — but vintners say drought years produce excellent wine.

The University of Michigan reversed its decision to cancel a campus screening of "American Sniper" after a backlash. More than 200 students had petitioned against the film, saying its portrayal of the Iraq War was negative toward Middle Eastern people. A university official called the cancellation a "mistake" inconsistent with freedom of expression; "Paddington" will be shown as an alternative.

Billboard runs down the hits and misses of the 2015 MTV Movie Awards. Highlights included host Amy Schumer's opening segment and monologue, Channing Tatum twerking onstage for Jennifer Lopez, Rebel Wilson's off-colour ad-lib, and Robert Downey Jr.'s Generation Award. Misfires included Schumer's botched archery gag, a poorly received "Gone Girl" joke, and Shailene Woodley's rambling Trailblazer speech.

Oregon officials towed a 20- to 30-foot fiberglass boat section into Newport harbor this week, suspected debris from Japan's March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. Biologists found yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters inside and deemed the invasive-species risk minimal. The boat remnants will be dried, inspected and landfilled, while the fish go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

Tuesday marked one year since Boko Haram militants seized 276 schoolgirls from a secondary school in Chibok, northeastern Nigeria; about 50 escaped and more than 200 remain missing.

Nigerian President-elect Muhammadu Buhari, who has pledged to crush the group, offered prayers for the victims, while Malala Yousafzai told the girls they would not be forgotten.

Boko Haram still holds territory in the northeast, and UNICEF says 800,000 children have been displaced by the conflict. Amnesty International reports abductions and killings continue.

A CNN opinion piece explains the Easter Triduum — Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday — plus its prologue, Maundy Thursday, arguing many Christians don't understand Holy Week's meaning. The author describes the crucifixion as suffering, Holy Saturday as anxious suspension, and the resurrection as total transformation rather than mere revival. He contends the three-day pattern recurs throughout human life and, unlike Christmas, has resisted commercialization.

Kenya has frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following last week's massacre of 147 people at a university in Garissa, with officials saying more could follow. The government also launched airstrikes on militant camps in Somalia and offered a $215,000 reward for alleged attack organiser Mohamed Mohamud. Hundreds gathered in Nairobi's Uhuru Park to mourn, as authorities faced criticism over reports that a rapid response team was delayed for hours awaiting transport.

Jia Jiang quit a six-figure job at 30 to pursue entrepreneurship, then launched a "100 Days of Rejection" blog project to confront his fear of being turned down after investors declined his tech start-up. A 2012 video of him asking a Krispy Kreme manager for Olympic-symbol doughnuts — she agreed — went viral, bringing talk show appearances, speaking invitations and job offers. His book "Rejection Proof" is released this week, arguing rejection can be turned into opportunity.

Attorney General Eric Holder issued a memo Friday barring all Justice Department personnel from soliciting, procuring or accepting commercial sex, even in jurisdictions where prostitution is legal. Holder said paying for sex fuels demand for human trafficking and threatens the department's core mission; violators face suspension or dismissal, on or off duty.

The directive follows an inspector general report that found DEA agents overseas attended sex parties with prostitutes paid for by drug cartels, and that such misconduct cases were poorly handled.

Authorities in Goldsboro, North Carolina, are investigating whether the fatal shooting of Wayne Community College print shop operator Ron Lane was a hate crime. Police say suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study student dropped from the program in March, shot Lane once with a shotgun Monday; relatives said Lane was gay, and investigators are examining possible ties between Stancil and a white supremacist gang. Stancil was arrested early Tuesday while sleeping on a beach in Daytona, Florida, and is expected to be returned to North Carolina to face charges.

Amnesty International's annual review found governments increasingly using the death penalty as a political response to crime and terrorism, with Pakistan, Jordan and Indonesia resuming or expanding executions and death sentences worldwide rising by more than 500 in 2014, largely due to Egypt and Nigeria. Despite this, recorded executions fell from 778 in 2013 to 607 in 2014, excluding China, where figures are a state secret. Amnesty notes 140 countries are now abolitionist in law or practice, up from eight in 1945, and argues there is no evidence executions deter crime more effectively than imprisonment.

A Duke University student has admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near a campus student union early Wednesday, officials said. The unidentified student is no longer on campus and faces student conduct review, while criminal investigations continue. Hundreds of students and faculty rallied in protest, with university President Richard Brodhead denouncing the act.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor who played senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law," died Sunday at his Santa Monica home after a long illness at age 86, his wife said. Dysart appeared in every episode of the 1986-94 series, winning the supporting actor Emmy in 1992 after four consecutive nominations. His other credits included "The Hospital," "Being There," "The Thing," "Pale Rider" and "Wall Street," plus stage work in "That Championship Season," for which he won a Drama Desk Award.

Easter marks Christ's crucifixion and resurrection, celebrated Sunday by Pope Francis in a rainy St. Peter's Square and at Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulcher. The holiday's date shifts annually — the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox — and Orthodox Christians, who follow the Julian calendar, celebrate a week later, explaining the timing of the recent blood moon. The Easter bunny and eggs likely originated in Germany, with the first written mention in 1682.

Comedian Chris Rock has tweeted photos of himself being pulled over by police three times in seven weeks, the latest early Tuesday with the message "Stopped by the cops again wish me luck." The posts drew widespread support online, though some accused him of race-baiting. Actor Isaiah Washington sparked backlash by advising Rock to "#Adapt," saying he sold his Mercedes for Priuses to avoid being stopped.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., the original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died in a single-car crash in Cartersville, Georgia, late Friday, Georgia State Patrol said. Burns, 64, was not wearing a seat belt when his car struck a mailbox and a tree. He was part of the band's original 1965 lineup and left in 1975, two years before the plane crash that killed frontman Ronnie Van Zant.

A viral photo of a cat on a staircase has sparked online debate over whether the animal is walking up or down, spawning the hashtag #UporDown. Uploaded to Imgur days ago, the image gained traction after a post on 9gag.com. Commenters have argued over the cat's direction of motion and the stairs' construction, and advertisers have jumped on the trend.

The US and its P5+1 partners reached a framework agreement with Iran in Lausanne, Switzerland, curbing Tehran's nuclear program to block a weapons capability. The deal would cut Iran's low-enriched uranium stockpile, reduce installed centrifuges by two-thirds and impose expanded IAEA inspections under a permanent Additional Protocol. Opponents in Congress and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu are expected to push back, though supporters say criticisms rest on dubious assumptions about the talks' objectives and terms.

Rolling Stone's retraction of its discredited UVA gang rape story leaves intact the undisputed core claim that the university has never expelled a student for sexual assault and faces ongoing scrutiny over its handling of cases, including a state-ordered review by O'Melveny & Myers and a federal Title IX investigation. Columbia Journalism School found the error could have been avoided had reporter Sabrina Rubin Erdely contacted "Jackie's" friends, who have since described a different account.

Survivors and advocates fear the retraction will deter victims from coming forward and has erased other students' testimony about a campus culture unsympathetic to victims, with some criticising the magazine for sensationalising an atypical case.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed in the abdomen and elbow early Wednesday near the 1OAK nightclub in Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood; his companion Katrine Saltara and another woman were also slashed. A 22-year-old Brooklyn man was arrested with charges pending, and Copeland is in stable condition.

Atlanta Hawks players Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, who were not involved in the stabbing, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges after allegedly interfering with police at the scene. Both will sit out Wednesday's game against the Nets and say they will contest the charges.

Twisted Sister has announced that its 2016 tour, marking the band's 40th anniversary, will be its last. The farewell trek is titled "Forty and F*ck It." Drummer Mike Portnoy of Adrenaline Mob replaces A.J. Pero, who died March 20, and the band will play two benefit shows in Pero's honor in Las Vegas and New Jersey.

John Travolta says he has no interest in seeing HBO's documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief," calling it "decidedly negative." The actor, a Scientologist for 40 years, said the film reflects the views of people "disgruntled with their experiences." Travolta credited the church with helping him cope with the 2009 death of his son Jett.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million over its opening weekend, with many viewers saying the film's tribute to late star Paul Walker moved them to tears. Walker died in a November 2013 car crash before filming was complete; body doubles, CGI and his brothers were used to finish his scenes. Director James Wan said producers chose to retire Walker's character rather than kill him off, ending with a montage set to Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth's "See You Again."

HBO's "Game of Thrones" returns Sunday for its fifth season, premiering simultaneously in 170 countries for the first time. Major story arcs are set to converge, with Stannis at the Wall and Tyrion's path expected to cross Daenerys'. The season will also move ahead of George R.R. Martin's novels, with the series slated to end after seven years.

CNN profiles several people who survived being lost at sea, including Louis Jordan, rescued off North Carolina after 66 days on his capsized sailboat, and Jose Salvador Alvarenga, who drifted across the Pacific for more than a year before washing up in the Marshall Islands.

Others include Hawaii fisherman Ron Ingraham, found alive 12 days after a search was called off, and Panamanian teenager Adrian Vasquez, rescued near the Galapagos after 26 days adrift in which his two companions died.

The article also cites Hiromitsu Shinkawa, swept nine miles out to sea by Japan's 2011 tsunami and rescued two days later clinging to his roof.

The first six "Star Wars" films arrive on digital HD Friday, bundled with special features. The extras include behind-the-scenes material on the saga's sound design. In one clip, sound designer Ben Burtt reveals the animal noises used to create the Geonosians' alien voices in "Attack of the Clones."

A Boston jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts related to the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings and the ensuing violence. Survivors and victims' families in the courtroom wept quietly as the verdicts were read, with many describing relief and accountability rather than celebration. Some, including amputee Rebekah Gregory, said no verdict could deliver full justice, and opinions remained divided over whether Tsarnaev should be sentenced to death.

Chinese prosecutors on Friday charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang, 72, with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets — making him the highest-ranking Communist Party official ever to face corruption charges. A former member of the Politburo Standing Committee who retired in 2012, Zhou was expelled from the party and arrested last December; his trial will be held in Tianjin. Analysts call Zhou the biggest "tiger" snared in President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption drive, though some see the case as the product of factional struggle.

A 21-year-old quadriplegic man with cerebral palsy was found in Philadelphia's Cobbs Creek Park after allegedly being left there for more than four days with only a blanket and a Bible. Police say his mother abandoned him Monday and travelled to Maryland to visit her boyfriend, telling family and officers her son was with her. He is hospitalised with dehydration, malnutrition, eye problems and an infected back wound; his mother was arrested in Maryland and faces charges including kidnapping and aggravated assault.

Walmart's opposition to Arkansas' religious freedom bill, coming weeks after it raised wages for 500,000 workers, marked the retailer as a bellwether of shifting public opinion in conservative states. Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson said he would not sign the bill unless its language was changed, hours after Walmart CEO Doug McMillon urged a veto.

Business backlash also forced Indiana Gov. Mike Pence to pledge changes to his state's law, while Republican presidential hopefuls split, with Jeb Bush softening his support and Ted Cruz attacking companies for following an "extreme left wing agenda."

A CNN writer describes abandoning her Catholic faith after a parish refused to let her speak to a priest following her 25-year-old brother's death from cancer. She says Pope Francis's humility and non-judgmental tone, including his remarks on gay people, have rekindled her belief. An interview with newly appointed Cardinal Gerald Lacroix of Quebec City, who stressed the church welcomes rather than rejects sinners, convinced her to return to Mass.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau, the former student she was jailed for having sex with in 1996, will mark their 10th wedding anniversary on May 20. The couple, now 53 and 31, discuss their marriage in an exclusive Barbara Walters interview airing Friday on ABC's "20/20." She says she hopes to teach again and have her sex offender status lifted, while he talks about alcoholism and depression.

Opinion piece argues Hillary Clinton's 2016 candidacy will unfairly become the measure of US gender equality. A win could prompt premature declarations of victory for women's political inclusion, while a loss would reinforce the myth that women can't win big races. Author contends Clinton is an atypical candidate with 23 years of name recognition and baggage, and that partisanship and the economy — not sexism — decide presidential elections.

Amnesty International's annual report says governments are invoking real or perceived terrorist threats to justify executions, citing Pakistan's lifting of a moratorium after the Peshawar school attack and China's "Strike Hard" campaign in Xinjiang.

Executions worldwide fell about 22% to at least 607 in 2014, excluding China, where figures are a state secret and thousands are believed killed. But death sentences rose 28% to at least 2,466, driven by mass sentencings in Egypt and Nigeria.

Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia executed more people than the United States, the only country in the Americas to carry out executions, with 35 in 2014.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani told parliament the country's Air Self Defense Force has never encountered an extraterrestrial UFO. He said jets scramble to inspect unidentified objects but have only found birds or non-alien aircraft. The response came to a question from lawmaker and former pro wrestler Antonio Inoki, who says he has seen a UFO himself.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films project about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt, Deadline reported. Wahlberg hopes to play former Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis, whose perspective will frame the story, which will draw on research and footage from "60 Minutes." It is the second Boston bombing film announced, after Fox's "Boston Strong."

Democratic long-shot presidential hopefuls Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb shared a stage at the Polk County Democrats dinner in Des Moines on Friday, meeting each other for the first time that day. The former Maryland governor worked the room and delivered an applause-laden stump speech, while the former Virginia senator stayed near his seat and gave a subdued, biographical address focused on governance, economic and criminal justice reform. Both trail far behind Hillary Clinton, polling at 1-3% as she prepares to announce her campaign.

Turkey's military said nine British citizens were arrested Wednesday at the Turkey-Syria border, suspected of attempting to cross illegally into Syria. The group comprised three men, two women and four children, the youngest born in 2013, all holding British passports, a Turkish official said. Britain's Foreign Office said it was seeking information from Turkish authorities.
