The US Justice Department has indicted FedEx on 15 counts, including conspiracy and money laundering, alleging the courier knowingly shipped drugs for illegal online pharmacies despite warnings from the DEA, FDA and Congress since 2004. FedEx denies wrongdoing, arguing it is shielded by the "common carrier" exception, which lets transport firms handle controlled substances in the normal course of business without liability. Unlike most companies, which settle via deferred prosecution agreements and fines, FedEx is contesting the charges and seeking dismissal.

Kenyans took to social media with the hashtag #147notjustanumber to share stories and photos of the 147 people killed in last week's Al-Shabaab attack on Garissa University College, as authorities have yet to release a victims' list. The dead included 142 students, three security officers and two university security staff, making it Kenya's deadliest attack since the 1998 US Embassy bombing. Churches held Easter memorial services under armed guard; one of the slain gunmen was identified as the son of a government chief in Mandera.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman is documenting fathers who take full advantage of the country's parental leave policy, which grants 480 days, including 60 reserved "daddy months" that are forfeited if unused. Only 12% of Swedish couples split the leave equally, with mothers still taking the bulk of it. Bavman, himself a father, has photographed 35 fathers so far and aims for 60 for a planned exhibition and book.

Obama told The New York Times he is "absolutely committed" to preserving Israel's military edge over Iran, and would pledge US support if Israel were attacked. The remarks follow criticism from Israeli PM Netanyahu and congressional Republicans of the framework nuclear deal with Tehran. Obama argued the accord is worthwhile even if Iran cannot be trusted, as it provides visibility into its nuclear activities. Talks on a final agreement run until June 30.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has drawn criticism that it licenses discrimination against gay people. Twenty states now have versions of the 1993 federal law, but experts say claims under them are rare and successful cases have mostly involved religious minorities rather than Christian denominations. Past cases include a Native American's seized eagle feathers, a Brazilian church's hallucinogenic tea, an Orthodox Jewish inmate's kosher meals, a Sikh IRS worker's ceremonial dagger, and a failed zoning challenge by Chicago churches.

Five young Chinese feminists detained in March face possible five-year prison terms on charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order," a lawyer for one of the women said. The women were held in Beijing, Guangzhou and Hangzhou shortly before planned International Women's Day events at which they intended to distribute anti-sexual harassment stickers. Their detention has sparked international protests, a "free the five" social media campaign and criticism from Hillary Clinton, prompting a rebuke from Beijing.

Selena's family is creating a digital, hologram-like version of the late Tejano singer, 20 years after her death, using technology from Nevada firm Acrovirt LLC. Dubbed "Selena the One," the project aims to release new songs and videos, collaborate with current artists and tour in 2018. An Indiegogo campaign seeking $500,000 launches April 16, ahead of the Fiesta de la Flor tribute event in Corpus Christi, Texas, on April 17-18.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to Andreas Lubitz, the Germanwings co-pilot accused of deliberately crashing Flight 9525, in a March 31 Facebook post criticising the Iran nuclear deal. She wrote Obama was "a deranged pilot flying his entire nation into the rocks," predicting "smoldering remains of American cities." Commenters on her page called the remarks despicable and a bid for relevance.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River" opens in limited US and UK release April 10, a year after a Cannes premiere that drew boos and harsh reviews. Gosling said the film grew out of speculative footage he shot of Detroit's Brewster-Douglass Projects before their demolition, with the script written during filming. He described the city as "dangerous" and full of "impending threat," but said dereliction "doesn't define Detroit," pointing to signs of rebirth such as the Heidelberg Project.

Yahya Rashid, a 19-year-old British national from northwest London, has been charged with terror offenses after being detained at Luton airport on arrival from Istanbul. He faces charges of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others to commit acts of terrorism between November 1 and March 31. He was due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe singer Vince Neil drew criticism this week for a poorly received rendition of "The Star-Spangled Banner" at a Las Vegas Outlaws Arena Football League game. His performance joins a long list of memorable anthem attempts, from Whitney Houston's acclaimed 1991 Super Bowl version to Roseanne Barr's 1990 rendition, which was booed and called "disgraceful" by President George H. W. Bush. Others include Jimi Hendrix's psychedelic 1969 Woodstock take and Michael Bolton's 2003 ALCS performance, during which he needed written lyrics.

Nearly 2,000 World War I soldiers' inscriptions have been discovered in an underground city beneath battlefields near Naours, France, about 120 miles north of Paris. National Geographic photographer Jeff Gusky, who is documenting the site, has recorded 1,821 names — about 40% Australian, most others British, 55 American and 662 untraced. The centuries-old quarry site was privately owned and off-limits until 2013, when a consortium of villages acquired operating rights to promote local history.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The ICC opened a preliminary examination in January into the situation there, potentially paving the way for war crimes investigations against Israelis, though Palestinians could also face counter-charges. Israel and the United States, both non-members, opposed the accession, while Human Rights Watch welcomed it.

Anthony Ray Hinton, 58, walked free from a Birmingham, Alabama, jail Friday after nearly 30 years on death row for the 1985 murders of two fast-food managers. A judge dismissed the charges at the state's request after firearms experts found the revolver linked to him could not be matched to the crimes. His attorney, Bryan Stevenson of the Equal Justice Initiative, called the case a "textbook example of injustice" driven by race, poverty and inadequate legal representation.

Commentary argues that large tax refunds — received by 8 in 10 US taxpayers, averaging nearly $3,000 — plus free online filing create a "happy ending" that masks the system's flaws, citing Nobel laureate Danny Kahneman's colonoscopy research showing pleasant endings shape overall memories. The author says the US income tax has become effectively a wage tax that penalises two-earner marriages, offers most filers no charitable deduction and lightly taxes the wealthy's capital income. Tax-prep firms benefit by upselling services such as audit protection to refund recipients.

Jordan Spieth leads the Masters by four shots after a steady third round, despite a double bogey at the 17th. Justin Rose sits second at 12 under, with Phil Mickelson on 11 under. Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy both finished at six under, with Woods insisting a comeback is still possible.

Liana Barrientos, 39, has been married 10 times — nine between 1999 and 2002 — and is believed to still be married to four men. She pleaded not guilty in the Bronx to two counts of offering a false instrument for filing, over a 2010 marriage license on which she claimed it was her "first and only" marriage. Prosecutors say the marriages were part of an immigration scam; she faces up to four years in prison and returns to court May 18.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, drew boycott calls and online abuse after its owners said they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding under the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The restaurant closed Wednesday after a Goshen woman allegedly tweeted about burning it down; police have recommended charges of harassment, intimidation and threats. A GoFundMe campaign backing the owners raised $842,387 by Friday.

Mindy Kaling's brother, Vijay Chokalingam, says he posed as African-American to gain admission to medical school as an undergraduate, and is now writing a book about it titled "Almost Black." Kaling reportedly told him the stunt brought "shame upon their family." Critics note Chokalingam received only one offer, from a school ranked around 60th, and that he also faced racial profiling by police and store clerks while posing as black.

Antarctica recorded a temperature of 63.5F (15.5C) on March 24 at Argentina's Esperanza Base on the continent's northern peninsula, possibly the highest ever logged there. The World Meteorological Organization is assembling a committee of about 10 climatologists and meteorologists to verify the reading, checking equipment, procedures and nearby station records. An official finding is expected by late summer or early fall.

The Obama administration says it is "not putting a timeframe on" an Iraqi-led operation to retake Mosul from ISIS, backing away from earlier US suggestions of an April or May assault involving up to 25,000 Iraqi troops. Officials cite progress against ISIS, including the recent recapture of Tikrit, but note Mosul is far larger — about a million people — and more strategically vital to the militants. Coalition airstrikes are already hitting ISIS positions near the city, though no US combat troops are planned and officials urged "patience."

Irish bookmaker Paddy Power has apologised after tweeting that Newcastle "have suffered more Kop beatings over the last 20 years than an unarmed African-American male," a reference to US police killings. The firm deleted the post and said "it was a joke, and no offense was meant," but social media users demanded the author be sacked. The company, known for publicity stunts, previously drew criticism for backing David Ginola's FIFA presidential bid and for a "money back if he walks" offer on Oscar Pistorius's trial.

Philadelphia police have added an attempted murder charge against Nyia Parler, 41, accused of abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in Cobbs Creek Park for more than four days while she travelled to Maryland to visit her boyfriend. The man, who also has cerebral palsy, was found Friday lying in leaves with a blanket, Bible and wheelchair nearby, suffering dehydration, malnutrition and a back wound. Parler, in custody in Montgomery County, Maryland, cannot be extradited until she completes an unspecified treatment.

Kim Ki-Jong has been charged with attempted murder, assaulting a foreign envoy and business obstruction over the March 5 knife attack on U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Mark Lippert, a Seoul court official said. Lippert required 80 stitches for a 10-centimeter facial gash and suffered cuts to his left arm and hand, but no permanent nerve or function damage is expected. Police said Kim, who had a 2010 suspended sentence for throwing concrete at Japan's ambassador, attacked Lippert in opposition to joint U.S.-South Korean military drills; his trial must begin within 14 days.

Jill (Duggar) Dillard, the first daughter married on TLC's "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth Monday to a son, Israel David, weighing 9 pounds, 10 ounces, People reported. The baby arrived more than a week past his due date. Her parents, Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar, posted a video of the new family on Facebook.

"Furious 7" is tracking for a $135 million-$138 million North American opening, the biggest domestic debut since November 2013 and the largest of 2015 so far. The film took a record $60 million internationally on Wednesday and Thursday, putting it on course for a worldwide bow near or above $300 million. It is Universal's widest release ever, playing in 4,003 US theaters and more than 10,500 screens across 63 territories, and is the last to feature Paul Walker, who died in a 2013 car crash during production.

A Secret Service supervisor, Xavier Morales, has been placed on administrative leave and had his security clearance suspended after a female subordinate accused him of making sexual advances and grabbing her arms during a struggle at the agency's office following a March 31 party. Director Joe Clancy called the allegations "very disturbing," saying workplace threats or violence "will not be tolerated." The case, to be probed by the Office of the Inspector General, is the latest in a string of scandals that have prompted a leadership change and warnings the agency is stretched "beyond its limits."

Hillary Clinton is launching her 2016 presidential bid, entering the race as one of the Democrats' strongest candidates in decades, with deep political and policy experience and a proven ability to weather partisan attacks and scandals. But analysts say she faces significant vulnerabilities: doubts about her authenticity and trustworthiness, tepid enthusiasm among the party's liberal base, persistent gender bias, and the risk of running an "inevitability" campaign like Al Gore's in 2000. Bill Clinton, while a formidable campaigner, also poses liabilities, including questions over Clinton Foundation fundraising and renewed scrutiny of his personal life.

The Justice Department will begin negotiations with Ferguson to overhaul its police force after finding a pattern of racial discrimination, including racist emails and predatory court fines. The city manager and police chief have resigned, and voters elected two black city council members, splitting the council evenly by race. Commentators say lasting reform depends on continued activism and on addressing governance flaws — weak elected officials and low-turnout off-year elections — common across St. Louis County and US suburbs.

Etihad Airways lost a US couple's two-year-old cat, Felix, after an April 1 flight from Abu Dhabi to New York's JFK Airport, with owner Jennifer Stewart saying the pet's plastic carrier arrived crushed and holed.

The cat remains missing nearly a week later. Etihad, which says pet losses are "extremely rare" and shipped over 200 animals last year, is investigating, has hired third-party specialists and pledged to review its pet handling procedures.

Stewart, who paid $1,200 to ship Felix, has enlisted a nonprofit's detection dog, while a wildlife biologist has set traps at the airport.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued by a container ship crew hundreds of miles offshore after 66 days adrift on his disabled 35-foot sailboat, which capsized three times and lost its mast after he set out from Conway, South Carolina. Jordan, who broke a shoulder, survived on collected rainwater and fish he netted after they were drawn to his laundry trailed in the water. Rescuers and his father said he was in surprisingly good condition; the Coast Guard says it has no reason to doubt his account.
